question: In a healthy newborn and young infant, right ventricular dominance on ECG (right axis deviation and dominant R wave in V1) is a normal finding reflecting the relative right ventricular preponderance at birth, and should NOT be interpreted as right ventricular hypertrophy.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is TRUE. Neonatal right ventricular dominance is physiological — it reflects the fetal haemodynamic state. The ECG of a healthy newborn NORMALLY shows right axis deviation and a dominant R in V1. Pathological RVH in a neonate is indicated by ADDITIONAL features such as a very tall R in V1 beyond expected norms, strain pattern, or clinical correlation with a structural defect.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. At birth, the right ventricle has been doing most of the work in fetal life (pulmonary resistance is high in utero). The newborn ECG normally shows: right axis deviation (QRS axis +90 to +180 degrees), dominant R in V1, and T-wave inversions in right precordial leads. This pattern gradually shifts toward left ventricular dominance over the first 3-6 months as pulmonary resistance falls and the left ventricle takes over. Misinterpreting normal neonatal RVD as pathological RVH leads to unnecessary investigation.
